summary: Specifies the PINT Service Protocol 1.0, which extends SIP and SDP so that a user on an IP network can invoke certain telephone services, such as asking for a call to be placed. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: PINT lets a program on the Internet ask the telephone network to do something, such as place a call or send a fax. The request travels as a SIP message and the description of the wanted call travels as SDP. The RFC adds extensions to those two protocols, and three new SIP methods so the requester can hear back about the result.

subtitle: How a program on the Internet asks the telephone network to place a call, send a fax or read out some content.

tldr.problem: Users, network operators and call centre providers all wanted to invoke ordinary telephone services, such as a callback or a fax, from an IP network, but there was no agreed way for an IP host to ask for one.
tldr.mechanism: PINT reuses SIP and SDP with extensions. A PINT client sends a SIP invitation whose SDP description names a telephone session, a network type of TN, a transport of voice, fax or pager, and where the content comes from. A PINT gateway relays the request into the telephone network, where an executive system performs it.
tldr.outcome: The result is a documented way for Internet applications to drive telephone services, plus three new SIP methods, SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and UNSUBSCRIBE, so the requester can find out how the service turned out. The protocol deliberately says little about the telephone side.

today: RFC 2848 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It is an extension of two other documents rather than a replacement: RFC 2543 for SIP and RFC 2327 for SDP. The RFC itself points back to RFC 2458, which describes the work on PINT that came before this specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The wish to invoke telephone call services from the Internet has been raised by users, public and private network operators, call centre service providers and equipment vendors. The generic scenario has three steps: an IP host sends a request to a server on an IP network, the server relays the request into a telephone network, and the telephone network performs the requested call service. A user who wants a callback placed to their telephone, or wants a weather warning read out by a remote automatic service, is asking for exactly that.

The RFC calls such a complete transaction a PINT Service, where PINT stands for PSTN/Internet Interworking. A PINT service always involves two separate networks: an IP network, which requests the placement of a call, and the Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN), which executes the actual call. Intelligent Network systems, private PBXs, cellular phone networks and ISDN can all be used to deliver PINT services, and the request may even come from within a private IP network that is disconnected from the whole Internet.

The requirements for PINT were deliberately restricted to a small number of fixed telephone call services, the Milestone services, so that the protocol could stay aligned with other Internet protocols and grow alongside Internet conferencing. PINT is specified as a set of enhancements and additions to SIP 2.0 and SDP: SIP establishes the association between the participants, and SDP describes the media to be exchanged within the session. PINT extends both so that the media in question is a telephone call rather than an Internet media session.

Three new SIP requests are added for PINT: SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. They let a client register interest in the outcome of a service, which matters because the person asking for a fax is often not the person it is sent to, and would otherwise have no easy way of finding out whether the transmission worked.
sections.plainLanguage: PINT lets a program on the Internet ask the telephone network to do something, such as place a call or send a fax. The request travels as a SIP message, and the description of the wanted call travels as SDP. The RFC adds extensions to those two protocols and three new SIP methods for hearing back about the result.

sections.title: The Milestone Services
sections.content:
Three telephone services are defined as the starting point.

The Request to Call service sends a request from an IP host that causes a phone call to be made, connecting party A to some remote party B. The Request to Fax Content service causes a fax to be sent to fax machine B; the request may contain a pointer to the fax data, which could reside in the IP network or in the telephone network, or the fax data itself, and the content may be text or a more general image. The Request to Speak, Send or Play Content service causes a phone call to be made to user A and for some content to be spoken out; that request must either contain a URL pointing at the content or include the content itself.

In all of these the details of the transmission stay inside the telephone network and are not accessible to the IP network. The fax service is not fax over IP: the IP network is only used to send the request that a certain fax be sent, and whether the resulting telephone call happens to use a real-time IP fax solution is completely transparent to the PINT transaction.

A PINT request deliberately does not pin down the exact telephone-side service. A request to call a number with thousands of agents in the call centre leaves open which agent returns the call, whether the agent's phone rings first or the user's, and what the user hears while waiting. Hundreds of fax protocol details are negotiated in the same way, along with transmission details within the telephone networks used. Those operational details are outside the scope of PINT, and a PINT system that wants to allow requests to carry such detail uses the SDP attribute mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: PINT starts with three services: place a call, send a fax, and read content out over the phone. The request says what should happen, but not how the telephone network arranges it, so a call centre can still pick its own agent and its own sequence of rings.

sections.title: Functional and Protocol Architecture
sections.content:
PINT clients and servers are SIP clients and servers. SIP carries the request over the IP network to the correct PINT server, in a secure and reliable manner, and SDP describes the telephone network session that is to be invoked or whose status is to be returned.

A PINT system uses SIP proxy servers and redirect servers for their usual purpose, but at some point there must be a PINT server with the means to relay received requests into a telephone system and to receive acknowledgement of those relayed requests. Such a server is called a PINT gateway, and it appears to a SIP system as a User Agent Server. To the PINT infrastructure it looks as if it represents a user, while in fact it represents an entire telephone network infrastructure that can provide a set of telephone network services.

A single PINT request may pass through a series of location servers, proxy servers and redirect servers before it reaches the PINT gateway that can actually process it. The gateway might have a true telephone network interface, or it might be connected through some other protocol or API to an Executive System capable of invoking services within the telephone cloud. In an Intelligent Network system the gateway might appear to realise the Service Control Gateway Function, and in an office environment it might be a server adjunct to the office PBX, connected to both the office LAN and the PBX. The Executive System that lies beyond the gateway is outside the scope of PINT.

Only two things are mandatory in PINT 1.0: the TN network type with its associated RFC2543 address type, and the require attribute. Every other new construct enables a different function, and a client or server that wants that function must use the construct the document specifies, so building a client and server that offer only the Request-to-Call service is allowed. Any other SIP or SDP option is available to PINT clients and servers without change, which is how a language preference, a requested time of day or a quality attribute is expressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The pieces are ordinary SIP servers, with one extra role: the PINT gateway, which relays a request into the telephone network and looks to SIP like a user agent. Behind it sits an executive system that actually performs the call, and that part is outside PINT's scope. Only two of the new pieces are mandatory, the TN address type and the require attribute.

sections.title: Extensions to SDP
sections.content:
PINT adds to SDP the ability to describe audio, fax and pager telephone sessions, and it deliberately hides the technical detail and complexity of the telephone network. The only network type defined for PINT is the generic TN, Telephone Network; more precise tags such as ISDN or GSM are not defined. The transport protocols are named simply voice, fax and pager, and the data to be transported is identified only by a MIME content type such as text, image or application data.

The address types allowed for network type TN are RFC2543 and private address types, which must begin with X-. An RFC2543 address is a string conforming to a subset of the telephone-subscriber syntax in SIP. It is either a global phone number, recognised by a leading plus sign and by default interpreted as an internationally significant E.164 number, or a local phone number given in the default dialling plan of the recipient PINT gateway. Examples in the RFC include c= TN RFC2543 +1-201-406-4090 and c= TN RFC2543 12014064090. A private address type is useful within a local domain, for example c= TN X-mytype.mydomain.com A*8-HELEN.

SDP has no way of describing a data object used as the source of a request, so PINT defines a fmtp attribute for each entry in the media format list. Each entry may resolve to a source in one of three ways, told apart by a leading tag: a uri: reference to a data object on the IP network, which should be an absolute URI; an opr: opaque reference to data held in the telephone network, which is sent untouched through the PINT infrastructure; or an spr: sub-part reference to a MIME part inside the request itself, given by its Content-ID. A request may mix the three, and the sources are sent as a sequence rather than in parallel.

Attribute lines carry further information into the telephone network. The phone-context attribute gives the network or private prefix that makes a local number meaningful, which is what lets a client reach a number that only works from inside one network. The clir attribute records whether the originator wants the calling line identity presented to the other party, which some jurisdictions require callers to be able to choose. Attributes of the form Q763- carry further parameters for a local phone number, such as the nature of address, the numbering plan, and whether routing to an internal network number is allowed.

Because SDP lets a server ignore attribute parameters it does not understand, a client that needs one to be honoured uses the require attribute, listing the attributes it requires. The server must then both understand each listed attribute and fulfil the request it implies. If it does not recognise the attribute it must return an error status code such as 420 Bad Extension or 400 Bad Request, and if it recognises the attribute but cannot fulfil the request it must reject with 606 Not Acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The session description says what kind of telephone session is wanted, using the network type TN, a transport of voice, fax or pager, and a telephone address. It can also point at the content to be sent, in three ways: by a URI on the Internet, by a reference to something held in the telephone network, or by a part of the message itself. A client that needs a particular attribute to be honoured can list it in the require attribute, so a server that does not understand it must refuse the request.

sections.title: Extensions to SIP
sections.content:
A PINT request can carry a multipart MIME payload. The first part must hold the SDP session description, including at least one of the format specific attributes for included content, and the later parts hold the content data. The Content Type of the enclosing SIP message must be multipart, and multipart/related is recommended. Requests that include data should be sent over TCP, because a proxy that forks a request carrying a large body would copy that body many times, and a client that does not yet know the gateway's location is advised to send a reference instead of the data itself.

A PINT server must support the SIP Warning header so that it can signal lack of support for individual PINT features, for example Warning: 305 pint.acme.com Incompatible media format: jpeg when it cannot retrieve and translate JPEG images into fax transmissions.

The three new methods register interest in the outcome of a service. SUBSCRIBE opens a monitoring session, and its state machine is the same as INVITE and BYE: INVITE signals the beginning and BYE the end of participation in a media session, SUBSCRIBE signals the beginning and UNSUBSCRIBE the end of participation in a monitoring session, and during the monitoring session the server sends NOTIFY messages about a change in session state or disposition. The session of interest is identified by the SDP origin field, the global session identifier, and the SUBSCRIBE request must not include any sub-part other than that session description. A successful response carries the session description as the gateway has it, and an Expires header says how long the monitoring session lasts; a value of 0 asks for one single immediate response. If the gateway no longer has a record of the session, it returns 606 Not Acceptable with the appropriate Warning 307 header saying the SDP session ID is no longer valid, so a client that wants information after the session ends should send its SUBSCRIBE before the session terminates. A NOTIFY carries the modified session description and may carry a Warning header and an information line, for example that three pages of five were sent.

The Require header lets a client demand a PINT extension, with the two tags org.ietf.sip.subscribe and org.ietf.sdp.require, and a client should use it only where it truly requires the server to reject the request if the option is not supported.

PINT URLs give the service a standard place to live. The user part of a SIP URL names the service, with R2C for Request-to-Call, R2F for Request-to-Fax and R2HC for Request-to-Hear-Content reserved for the milestone services, and the host part holds the domain name of the PINT service provider. A new URL parameter, tsp, names the actual telephone network provider to be used, for example INVITE sip:R2F@pint.pintservice.com;tsp=telco.com SIP/2.0.

REGISTER works as it does in SIP: a PINT gateway registers the service it can offer, and several gateways may register the same service so that a proxy can choose between them. Because one provider could otherwise release another provider's registration and divert its requests, all registrations by PINT gateways must be authenticated.

BYE needs extra precision. If a client sends BYE, the telephone call should end, but that is not always possible, for example when a fax is already in progress or the whole call has finished. In that case the server must return 606 Not Acceptable with a session description that indicates the telephone network session causing the problem, and a combination of Warning headers and information lines can describe the problem precisely.
sections.plainLanguage: On the SIP side, PINT adds a way to send the content inside the request, a Warning header for saying what is not supported, and three methods for monitoring the outcome: SUBSCRIBE to start watching, NOTIFY for news, and UNSUBSCRIBE to stop. It also fixes what a PINT URL looks like and what a BYE means when the telephone call cannot be stopped.

sections.title: Examples of PINT Requests and Responses
sections.content:
The RFC works through a set of complete requests. An anonymous user asking a call centre to call back sends INVITE sip:R2C@pint.mailorder.com SIP/2.0 with a session description whose media line is m=audio 1 voice - and whose connection line is c=TN RFC2543 +1-201-406-4090. The telephone number to be called is the one in the To header, and the plus sign marks it as an internationally significant E.164 number in the North American numbering plan.

A named customer asking to be called back by a particular sales agent sends INVITE sip:marketing@pint.mailorder.com SIP/2.0, with the agent's address in the To header. An implementation that cannot accept email-like URLs in the To header must decline the request with 606 Not Acceptable. The telephone-side details, such as whether the agent's phone rings first or the customer's, may be expressed in attribute lines, although specifying such lines for service consistency is beyond the PINT 1.0 specifications.

A customer asking to have the assembly instructions sent back by fax sends INVITE sip:faxback@pint.mailorder.com SIP/2.0 with a To header of sip:1-800-3292225@steam.edu;user=phone;phone-context=+1 and a media line of m=application 1 fax URI. In the fax and hear-content services the source of the content is given in an a=fmtp: line, as a URI reference, an opaque reference or a sub-part reference, while a request-to-call normally has no source at all.

The parameter summary near the end of the RFC ties the services to the fields that carry them: the service identifier goes in the user part of the Request-URI, the A party in the To header, the B party in the SDP connection line, the call format in the transport protocol of the media line, and the source and its format in the media type and the fmtp attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a request to call, a request to be called back, and a request for a fax-back. Together they show where each piece of the request goes: the service name in the request line, the parties in the To header and the connection line, and the content in the media and fmtp lines.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is the longest part of the RFC, and it starts from the risks of a request that causes a real call. The request can specify an incorrect telephone or fax number, the requestor can deliberately enter the number of an innocent third party, and the request can be intercepted on its way through the PINT or SIP infrastructure and altered. In any of these cases a call may be placed incorrectly, which may amount to harassment of the person who receives it, and someone may be liable for mistaken calls. The gateway must therefore not pass on a request unless it is sure the request has not been corrupted in transit, and a service provider may need to confirm the identity of the requestor, because in many jurisdictions operators must be able to identify the parties to a call, for example to carry out a malicious call trace.

Authority to make a request matters too, because the person paying for the call is often not the requestor, as with freephone numbers where the recipient pays. The authority a request carries should be treated as if it were financial information, such as a credit card number or PIN, since an eavesdropper could steal it and use it in their own requests.

Registration deserves care as well. Any number of gateways may register for the same service, and the standard SIP way of releasing a registration is a REGISTER request with a wildcard Contact and an expires value of zero. Without authentication one provider could release another provider's registration and take its requests, so all registrations by PINT gateways must be authenticated, including new registrations and cancellations.

The summary is blunt: PINT always carries data items that are sensitive, and there may be financial considerations as well as the usual privacy concerns, so the transactions must be protected from interception, modification and replay in transit. Unlike plain SIP, where requests and responses may be protected, PINT messages must be, so implementations must support SIP security. Where a network layer, transport layer or physical security mechanism already protects all the traffic, messages may be exchanged without SIP security, and clients and servers should support configuring that by hand.

Two consequences are worth knowing. The Request-URI and To header fields cannot be protected by SIP techniques, because proxies have to read them to route the request, so the telephone number of one party to a PINT call is visible to any interception, and transport or network layer protection must be used if those numbers are sensitive. And if the message body is encrypted, a proxy cannot read it to choose the right gateway, so a proxy should be ready to try another gateway when it receives a 501 or 415 rejection, which in turn opens a way to waste a gateway's effort with requests it cannot serve.
sections.plainLanguage: A PINT request can make a real phone call to the wrong person, so the RFC says the request must be protected from interception, change and replay, not merely left optional as it is in plain SIP. The number in the To header cannot be hidden from proxies, though, so a network or transport layer tunnel is needed when the numbers are private.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The final section is informative and describes how PINT might be built. Because there are many web browsers and servers, some PINT systems will use HTML and HTTP as a front end: the browser talks to an intermediate web server, which is closely associated with a PINT client, and that client represents the requesting user to the PINT gateway and onwards to the executive system.

Several gateways may be able to serve the same request, so a proxy or redirect server may have to choose between them, and a gateway that registers the same service as another can take requests that were meant for its rival. A registration database with several gateways registered for one service leaves the registrar free to pick whichever it likes, which is one more reason registrations have to be authenticated.

The section also collects the parameters needed to describe a traditional telephone service request fully, in a table that says which of the service identifier, the A party, the B party, the call format and the source are required for each of the four services, Request-to-Call, Request-to-Fax, the fax-back variant of Request-to-Fax, and Request-to-Hear-Content. It then maps each of those parameters onto the field that carries it in a PINT message.
sections.plainLanguage: The last section is advice for builders. It covers using a web page as the front end, choosing between several gateways that offer the same service, and the table that says which pieces each service needs and which PINT field carries each one.
